Trump administration seeks to restrict internships for international students
description: (This Aug 27 story has been republished, with no changes to text.)
fullText:
(This Aug 27 story has been republished, with no changes to text.)

WASHINGTON, Aug 27 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration has issued a memo for universities that seeks to restrict issuance of certain internship work ‌authorizations for international students as the federal government warned that colleges not complying with the regulations may lose certification ‌to enroll foreign students.

The federal memo dated August 24 said the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, which is part of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement ​agency, has "observed a rise in Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorizations that appear to violate regulatory requirements which permit CPT only where the training is an integral part of an established curriculum."

"Failure to comply with SEVP regulations may result in an institution losing certification to enroll foreign students," the memo said.

It resulted in some schools, including the University of California, Los Angeles and the University of California, Berkeley, pausing certain ‌applications for work authorizations for international students.

"UCLA ⁠has paused certain Curricular Practical Training authorizations while it reviews recent federal guidance and determines next steps," a UCLA spokesperson said.

UC Berkeley's international office said the August 24 memo was "more narrow in focus, more ⁠direct, and includes content that is more restrictive in nature." The federal government had also issued an earlier memo in mid-August.

UC Berkeley's international office said it is unlikely that it will process certain work authorization applications "in the near future" and urged those international students to plan ​accordingly.

It said ​it will continue processing "degree-requirement" CPT as normal and would resume processing "Doctoral ​Dissertation and Master's Thesis Research CPT." The office said ‌it would consult legal experts to develop new processes aligning with new federal requirements.

"Nothing about these regulations has changed," the Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent, said in a statement. "However, schools and employers should consider themselves on notice: under President Trump, abuse of this generous system will no longer be tolerated."

Trump has targeted universities with probes and funding threats over issues like pro-Palestinian protests against U.S. ally Israel's assault on Gaza, diversity initiatives, climate programs and transgender policies. Rights advocates have raised free speech, academic freedom ‌and due process concerns.

Separately, the U.S. Justice Department alleged on Thursday admissions ​practices at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Services favored ​Black and Hispanic applicants, citing findings of a probe ​as the Trump administration continued its diversity crackdown.

"We are disappointed by the DOJ's conclusions, which we believe ‌are incorrect," the university said, saying the admissions policies ​were in compliance with law and ​not discriminatory.

The Justice Department has alleged similar bias at other schools, saying the department aims for settlement talks. If those efforts fail, the department will file suit, it said.

Trump's administration has also revoked visas of student protesters over pro-Palestinian ​protests that it casts as antisemitic and ‌sympathetic to extremists.

Protesters, including some Jewish groups, say opposition to Israel's assault on Gaza and its occupation of ​Palestinian territories is not antisemitic and advocacy for Palestinian rights is not the same as supporting extremism.

Democratic strategist: ‘Something’s going on’ when Trump ‘can only deliver 52 percent’ in South Carolina
description: Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha said Wednesday he expected President Trump’s endorsement of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to lead to a wider margin of victory for her in Tuesday’s GOP Senate runoff. ...
fullText:
Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha said Wednesday he expected President Trump's endorsement of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to lead to a wider margin of victory for her in Tuesday's GOP Senate runoff.

Rocha explained in an appearance on NewsNation's "Cuomo" that he thought Graham would win but "didn't think it would be this close" given Trump backed the senator.

She defeated Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) by just less than 5 points in the state's runoff, securing a spot on the general election ballot in place of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

The GOP nominee will now face Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election, with Decision Desk HQ giving the Republican an 81 percent chance to win as of Tuesday.

Rocha, who advised Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) during his two unsuccessful presidential campaigns, noted that Darline Graham's narrow runoff victory does not lead him to believe Andrews will win.

"But I am going to say something's going on when Donald Trump can only deliver 52 percent," he told host Chris Cuomo, while qualifying, "I get it was a special election. She's only been running a little bit."

The strategist also noted more than 40 percent of voters in June's GOP primary voted for a candidate other than Lindsey Graham, an election held just more than a month before the four-term senator died of an aortic dissection.

"But Donald Trump should be getting 70, 80, 90 percent in a Republican primary," Rocha argued.

The president hit the trail last week to stump for Darline Graham, venturing to the coastal town of Myrtle Beach, S.C. During a rally alongside the newest senator, he urged Republicans to turn out in the midterms.

"What I want you to do is pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," Trump said at the time.

Graham won Horry County, where Myrtle Beach is located, by more than 46 points over Norman. The senator was also victorious in 34 of 46 counties in the Palmetto State, according to data from the South Carolina Election Commission.

The victory was seen as a significant flex by Trump after Graham made a major gaffe a week earlier on the debate state while dodging a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea.

More than 369,000 Republicans in the state cast a ballot in the runoff, accounting for roughly 12 percent of the more than 3 million total registered voters in the state, per the state election commission.

Democrats have suggested Graham's win could give their party a chance at taking the seat, though that appears unlikely.

Conservative talk show host Mark Davis, who also appeared as a guest on Cuomo's show, defended the GOP hopeful as being the "deep underdog" in the race "because nobody knew who she was on July 10, the day before Lindsey died."

"For Trump to endorse her and bring her across the finish line is a major, major bit of evidence to the strength of his endorsement," he added.

title: Florida grand jury finds DeSantis administration misused $10 million, but no charges filed
description: A Florida grand jury found that Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' administration “misappropriated” $10 million in taxpayer money it diverted to a charity connected to his wife, but it declined to file cri...
fullText:
A Florida grand jury found that Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' administration "misappropriated" $10 million in taxpayer money it diverted to a charity connected to his wife, but it declined to file criminal charges due to a lack of evidence indicating who specifically was responsible.

DeSantis on Thursday did not dispute the legitimacy of the secret grand jury report obtained and published online by CBS News Miami, but he insisted no laws were broken and said whoever leaked the sealed documents would face "consequences."

The Leon County grand jury completed its report in January on investigations into Hope Florida, the charity started in 2021 by Florida first lady Casey DeSantis. Despite the lack of charges, the report ignited a new round of criticism aimed at DeSantis and other top state Republicans over the charity receiving $10 million from a state Medicaid settlement intended to help poor children get health insurance.

David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor, called for the grand jury probe to be reopened. He faces Republican Byron Donalds in November. DeSantis, under Florida law, cannot seek a third term.

The Hope Florida charity is supposed to help financially struggling families connect with churches and aid groups to help keep them off publicly-financed assistance programs. The $10 million was instead moved to political action committees that used the money to oppose a 2024 statewide ballot measure that would have legalized marijuana for adults in the state.

DeSantis opposed the measure, and it fell just short of the 60% supermajority it needed to become law.

"Despite our finding that the money was misappropriated, we find insufficient evidence to charge anyone criminally," the report concluded.

The grand jury said no one would take responsibility for sending the money to the charity or had any memory of who did.

"We recognize that this would be an impediment to criminal prosecution," the report noted. "While we can't prove who is responsible, we can plainly see that taxpayer money was misused for political purposes and we would like to see changes made to prevent this from happening again."

The grand jury report concluded that James Uthmeier, who was DeSantis' chief of staff at the time, "was in a position of authority over those involved in settling," and that his Keep Florida Clean PAC was the prime recipient of the $10 million. The grand jury said then-state Attorney General Ashley Moody's office knew of the plans to divert the money. She was later appointed by DeSantis to the U.S. Senate.

Uthmeier and Moody are both seeking reelection.

In a news conference Thursday, Uthmeier suggested Democrats were behind the grand jury report leak and called renewed interest in its findings "a politically motivated hoax."

In a post on X on Thursday, Moody said her office was only one of several agencies that signed off on the initial settlement, and "had no knowledge of how funds would be spent" by Hope Florida, state lawmakers or any other group.

title: Fed will have "work to do" if inflation doesn't fade, Warsh says
description: Fed chief Kevin Warsh said in a closely watched speech that inflation remains a concern, while praising the broader U.S. economy.
fullText:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh reaffirmed the central bank's commitment to lowering consumer prices, acknowledging that inflation remains too high in a highly anticipated speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

During remarks at the Fed's annual conference, Warsh said that recent government data shows inflation has cooled, but "they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved."

While stopping short of saying the Fed could raise its benchmark interest rate, Warsh also signaled that policymakers are prepared to act if inflationary pressures don't subside. Inflation has eased in recent months after reaching a 3 -year high in May, but prices remain stubbornly above the Fed's 2% annual target.

"We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed," Warsh said. "Otherwise, we have work to do."

Although inflation remains hot, Warsh said he is "impressed by the overall performance of the economy," touting measures such as the nation's unemployment rate, which sat at 4.1% in July.

Economists and Wall Street analysts have looked for a clear signal from Warsh on how he thinks the Fed should respond to stubborn inflation. The Fed chair, who succeeded Jerome Powell, has been significantly more tight-lipped than his predecessors.

During the speech on Friday, Warsh again made the case for limiting forward guidance on future Fed policy decisions, which he has argued limits the central bank's flexibility by committing it to a specific policy path.

"Forward guidance as a regular practice was adopted by my colleagues and me during the Global Financial Crisis," he said. "It was essential at the time, and we introduced it with much fanfare. But, as with other legacies of crises past, I believe that the practice has overstayed its welcome."

Warsh has been less interested in telling markets what the Fed will do and more interested in explaining how the Fed reacts to changing conditions, Jasmine Yu, chief investment officer at Bryn Mawr Trust, told CBS News in an interview on Thursday.

While Warsh has sidestepped questions about the trajectory of interest rates, several Fed officials have underscored their openness to a rate hike. On Friday, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed a 55% likelihood that the Fed would raise rates at its Sept. 15-16 meeting.

title: Republican governor asks his AG to look into ‘aggressive’ behavior by Trump admin’s election monitors
description: Wyoming’s Republican Gov. Mark Gordon voiced concerns about the Justice Department election monitors who observed the primary election in his state last week, saying he’s asked his attorney general to...
fullText:
Wyoming's Republican Gov. Mark Gordon voiced concerns about the Justice Department election monitors who observed the primary election in his state last week, saying he's asked his attorney general to look into their "aggressive" behavior.

The Justice Department sent two Civil Rights Division attorneys to Laramie County, Wyoming, which includes the state capital of Cheyenne. But some officials, including the state attorney general, weren't made aware of the move in advance, Gordon said at a state canvassing board meeting Wednesday.

"It sounded like the behavior of the observers was a bit aggressive," Gordon said, adding, "It just was irregular and, and I have asked the attorney general to start looking into … the nature of the visits and all that sort of stuff."

The DOJ, when reached for comment, pointed CNN to an August 18 statement from Wyoming US Attorney Darin Smith: "Voters deserve absolute confidence that their ballots are secure and their voices are heard without interference…. We are working alongside local officials to ensure every lawful vote is protected."

CNN has reached out to the governor's office for comment.

The DOJ said it has sent more than 80 monitors to seven states so far this year for primary elections, as of Tuesday. The department has said it would send about 1,000 monitors to polling sites in November.

Gordon's criticism comes as President Donald Trump continues to sow doubt about elections. Earlier this year, he baselessly alleged there was cheating in the Los Angeles mayoral primary election before the DOJ sent a prosecutor to observe ballot processing. The president also still claims, without evidence, that the 2020 election he lost to former President Joe Biden was rigged.

Democrats and voting rights activists raised concerns last year, ahead of the off-year elections, that the monitors could be used to undermine the voting process or as a precursor to sow doubts about the election. But the Trump administration had insisted monitors are being sent out in line with decadeslong federal monitoring practices.

Gordon said he isn't against the idea of election monitors, but raised concerns that the "behavior" of the ones deployed to Wyoming "seemed to exceed what the authority that Congress had given them was."

"I'm not saying anything went wrong or anything else, and I certainly think that the conduct of this election was phenomenal," Gordon said. But, he added, "I don't like the federal government coming in and taking our votes."

CNN's Hannah Rabinowitz and Fredreka Schouten contributed to this report.

title: US academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism allowed to resume some work
description: Nathan Cofnas, the U. academic who accused late Cambridge University professor Jason Arday of plagiarism, has been allowed ‌to resume some of his work at Ghent University whi...
fullText:
PARIS, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Nathan Cofnas, the U.S. academic who accused late Cambridge University professor Jason Arday of plagiarism, has been allowed ‌to resume some of his work at Ghent University while a disciplinary ‌probe continues, the Belgian entity said on Friday.

Arday, once hailed as Cambridge's youngest Black professor, was ​found dead at the age of 41 in London this month, days after resigning from his post. Arday had denied the allegation of plagiarism but acknowledged making mistakes.

Ghent University subsequently suspended Cofnas "as a precautionary measure" as it opened an investigation. Cofnas said the ‌probe was into possible discrimination.

In ⁠Friday's statement, Ghent said Cofnas could resume academic activities at the university while the investigation continued on the condition that he worked ⁠remotely and did not engage in any teaching.

The plagiarism allegations against Arday drew huge media coverage, leading to questions about other elements of Arday's life, including statements he made ​about his ​career, personal life and medical conditions.

GHENT SAYS ​IT HAD CONTACT WITH U.S. AMBASSADOR

Ghent ‌also said it had been in contact with the U.S. ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, about Cofnas.

"Ghent University confirms that it has been in contact with the U.S. Ambassador," it said via email, confirming a social media post by White.

Cofnas wrote in a post on X late on Thursday that his suspension period was over, ‌thanking White for taking an interest in his ​case.

Cofnas arrived at Ghent after Cambridge University's Emmanuel ​College ended its association with him ​after some students expressed concerns over Cofnas' blog posts, which argued ‌that in a meritocracy "blacks would disappear ​from almost all high-profile ​positions outside of sports and entertainment".

Cofnas says he is not a racist and is in legal dispute with Emmanuel College.

Arday's death triggered intense debate about ​racism in the academic ‌world and the media in Britain.

Before his death, Arday repeatedly said the ​public attacks upon him were taking a toll on him and his ​family.

title: How does Larne's European exit impact Irish League?
description: BBC Sport NI takes a look at some of the key questions and possible setbacks following Larne's result.
fullText:
It has been a European campaign to forget for Irish Premiership teams this season.

After Linfield and Glentoran's first-round exits and Coleraine's hammering in the second round, Larne's European adventure ended in dramatic fashion.

The Inver Reds had a two-goal advantage following the first leg of their Uefa Conference League play-off, but a disastrous final 10 minutes at Inver Park saw Lincoln Red Imps score twice and Larne reduced to 10 men before the away side netted the winner in the final minute of extra time.

For Gary Haveron's side, the immediate consequences are obvious but, for the Irish League, the repercussions could be felt for years.

BBC Sport NI takes a look at some of the key questions and possible setbacks following Larne's exit.

One of the biggest concerns throughout the qualifying campaign has been Northern Ireland's coefficient ranking and what a poor European return could mean for the number of places available for Irish Premiership clubs.

Currently, the Premiership winners, runners-up, the play-off winners and the Irish Cup victors secure a European qualifying spot.

However, with it now highly likely that the Irish League will lose the fourth place and all the incentives that come with it, it is unclear how the league will readjust.

Irish League supporters may suddenly now find themselves keeping a much closer eye on teams and countries that may not have normally followed such as Georgia's Iberia 1999.

NI currently still sit 50th in the coefficient on 6.625 and if Iberia 1999 are defeated in all six of their Conference League fixtures, Georgia could not leapfrog Northern Ireland in the standings.

They have been drawn against FC Copenhagen, Red Star Belgrade, Getafe, Sint-Truiden, Jablonec and Mjallby AIF.

Liechtenstein will also be of interest next season with their rankings set to fall after their clubs' years of struggling to collect points in European competition.

Another consequence will be that the Irish Cup winners will also now be drawn into the first round of Uefa Conference League, not the second with all implications to come into play in the 2028-29 season.

The potential loss of the fourth European place would also raise questions around the final match of the season, the European play-off.

As things stand, teams who finish between third and seventh compete in a play-off for the final position European position.

However, Northern Ireland Football League [NIFL] chief executive Gerard Lawlor had suggested that if there became three European spots, the play-off may not take place.

"We would need to talk to the clubs about that and have a discussion, but it is probably the most sensible and easy outcome," he said when asked would the play-off be cancelled.

"We will give the club different models, but it is the reality we must adapt to."

Howver, with the excitement that the play-offs bring, managers such as Larne's Gary Haveron believe they are crucial.

"There are so many dead rubber games at the end of the season and if you are in the bottom half of the table and not involved in the Irish Cup, what is your motivation," Haveron told BBC Sport NI.

"What is the motivation if you cannot chase down seventh place and a European spot?

"The play-off has led to loads of excitement. Do I like being involved in them? No, but I have been involved in two finals, and the drama is absolutely unbelievable."

Had Larne qualified they would have received approximately £2.75 million in participation money for reaching the league stage of the Conference League and that figure could have risen with positive results.

The rest of the Premiership clubs would have benefited as well and received a six-figure solidarity payment.

For Larne, the loss of that revenue is particularly significant. The club will now have to reassess its spending both on the pitch and behind he scenes without the European windfall which they came so close to securing.

However, there is no doubt there will be an impact beyond Inver Park and into the league as well.

When Larne made history by becoming the first team from Northern Ireland to reach the group stages of a European competition, the 11 other Irish League clubs shared a financial windfall of over two million.

That money can make a huge difference from expanding facilities or developing players.

Another Larne run in the league phase could therefore have provided another boost across the Premiership.

Whenever Northern Irish clubs struggle in Europe, the debate over summer football normally returns.

Currently during the qualifiers, clubs from Northern Ireland are out of season, while many clubs are already mid-campaign by the time of July qualifiers.

Earlier in August, Lawlor said he hoped to discuss summer football with clubs before Christmas, with a view to a vote over changing the Irish League calendar as soon as the 2028-29 season.

However, it is an issue which divides opinion and no team from the Republic of Ireland, who play from mid-February to early November, qualified for the group stages of a European competition either this season.

It will take a few years the full implications of the lack of European involvement of teams from Northern Ireland to be felt, but it is clear that something must change to avoid this happening again for seasons to come.

title: Dunfermline v Raith preview - watch Fife derby on BBC tonight
description: Raith Rovers have made a fast start to the new Scottish Championship season. Dougie Imrie's side face Fife rivals Dunfermline Athletic on Friday - live on BBC Scotland.
fullText:
From a "pretty bleak" squad to players suddenly feeling the love, a flying Raith Rovers side go into Friday's Fife derby second in the Championship as they take on Dunfermline Athletic live on BBC Scotland.

Dougie Imrie's side are unbeaten in the league with two wins and a draw from their three league outings so far.

They were also unbeaten in regulation time through their League Cup group stage matches, but failed to progress to the last 16.

Despite their impressive form, Imrie played down Raith's promotion credentials.

"We're delighted with the start, but we'll not get carried away," Imrie said.

"We had a couple of tough weeks at the start of pre-season, picking up injury to players and having to go with a pretty bleak squad.

"But I think my experience and time at Morton has helped me in this situation. A lot of those seasons at Morton I was carrying 13 or 14 players through the League Cup leading into a league campaign."

The addition of winger Scott Tiffoney - a proven star at Championship level with Partick Thistle, and a player Imrie had been chasing since January - was a significant coup for the Kirkcaldy side.

And while injuries to striker George Oakley and winger Aaron Lyall have provided challenges, Imrie is happy with the overall picture.

"The most important thing in any football club is the environment," he said.

"One of the things I try to do is make the environment the best it can be, so knows everybody knows they are loved, they've got an opportunity to be in my team, make them believe they are good players.

"We certainly have a good squad. They have all really integrated well. I've brought in 11 players this summer and let 13 go so you have to quickly gel that together.

"The key is everybody knowing they have an opportunity to play in my team, but they also know they have to be at it every day to keep that jersey."

Dunfermline v Raith Rovers on Sportscene

Dunfermline made the play-offs last season and reached the Scottish Cup final, where they lost to Celtic.

They have started the new league campaign in sluggish fashion though, with two draws followed by defeat last weekend at Livingston.

The Pars did reach the last 16 of the League Cup - with a victory over Premiership St Mirren along the way in the group stage - but were knocked out at home by League 1 Ross County.

Despite their mixed fortunes, Lennon believes his side has what it takes to be potential Championship winners.

"It's my ambition. I think we'll be in the mix at the end of the season for sure," he said.

"We've recruited well. I think it takes time for players to bed in. 10 went out and nine came in, so it's a big overhaul.

"I'm excited about the players we have brought in and I'm excited by the style of play that we can produce as well.

"It's obviously taking a little bit more time than we would have wanted but it's not terminal or anything like that. This is only our fourth league game.

"Couple of wins and we'll be looking down the table rather than up."

title: 'They are now athletes' - how do referees get ready for a season?
description: Pre-season camps in Spain and full-time training throughout the season - the rigorous regimes top-flight officials undergo to keep up with the pace of play in the Premier League
fullText:
Referees know every decision will be scrutinised.

Fans, pundits and players will pore over their calls, creating never-ending debates.

Many of the Professional Referee Group, the top officials in the country, have met in Loughborough this week.

They meet every few weeks to work and train together, with the officials spread across the country.

Lunch is a choice of chicken, teriyaki beef or tofu with vegetables and salad, with protein bars and rice cakes alongside the fruit, granola and Greek yogurts.

It is a reminder of the environment. Since becoming professional in 2001 top flight officials have had to adapt.

"I never thought referees did as much as what we do now," says Sam Allison, who played for Chippenham Town and Frome Town during his playing career, which started at Swindon.

"We are training full-time, sometimes two, three sessions a day, making sure that we are ready on a Saturday afternoon.

"Some of it (not understanding referees' workload) is probably ignorance, lack of awareness, lack of communication being disseminated to people out there.

"I think of my ignorance of just thinking referees just turned up, refereed the game and then went home.

"We have all the preparation, all the training, all the sacrifices, all the commitment, all the desire, all the support networks, people investing in you to make sure that you are ready in the best position to deliver a game."

Allison, a former firefighter, is the fourth official for Manchester City's trip to Crystal Palace on Friday while colleague Sam Barrott has been given Saturday's early match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest.

Barrott took charge of Arsenal's Community Shield win over Manchester City this month and was in the Faroe Islands on 20 August to referee Ki Klaksvik's 0-0 draw with Riga in the Europa Conference League.

Different teams and different tactics means a different approach to each game, with officials prepping with Pro Ref's analysis team who provide key information to understand the way a team is going to play, to support the flow of the game.

It comes after a summer of work to ensure the officials can match - and better - the demands of the Premier League.

"At the moment we've got five substitutions and we see all the time fresh legs for teams can change the momentum in a game," said Barrott.

"If three new attacking players are on that are all very pacey after 70 minutes you know they're going to change the way they play, they're going to try and push.

"That normally means an increase in output for us and when that happens, there's not a point in us where we go, we can't handle this'.

"We've been trying to push the demands of where we are, everybody's trying to get better. Football has the 1% gains, every game or every training session we're very similar in the mindset, we want to be better."

Francis Bunce has been with Pro Ref - rebranded from the Professional Game Match Officials Limited - for 10 years and is now the physical performance manager.

He was with the group in Spain last month for their pre-season training camp, putting them through what is viewed as the infamous Maximal Aerobic Speed (MAS) test - an all out six-minute run.

"When you look at refereeing in the Premier League and Championship people very rarely talk about their physical qualities or physical capabilities," he tells BBC Sport.

"They've all done so well to keep developing and they look like athletes on the pitch - they are athletes.

"We're in a very different space with match officials, they are naturally some years older than the players and you can't get away from that because having a 21-year-old referee would be very difficult in the Premier League with everything you need to learn and experience.

"They should be definitely considered as athletes and if you then compare them to Joe Public who might want to shout some views from the sidelines, they wouldn't be able to keep up for a minute with what some of our guys can do."

With officials training remotely for part of the week, they need to be monitored with heart rate and GPS technology.

All the officials are on tailored plans and work in a group of around five once or twice a week at local hubs where strength and conditioning sessions are delivered.

Those at the World Cup - referees Michael Oliver and Anthony Taylor, along with assistants Gary Beswick, Adam Nunn, Stuart Burt and James Mainwaring - also had special training this summer, running and cycling in chambers of around 40 degrees to prepare them for the intense heat at the tournament.

Last season referees ran a total of 3.6m metres, with their overall sprint distance 12,136m.

At the weekend, Stuart Attwell covered the fourth highest distance of anyone on the pitch while taking charge of Newcastle's 2-2 draw with Liverpool, awarding the Reds a stoppage time penalty.

He was also fifth for highest high-speed running, therefore beating all but four players.

"A lot of people could go and run around the pitch but they wouldn't be able to pick up those key positions to make those defining decisions," says Bunce.

"That's something that's really important we build into our training, in terms of how we improve speed, how we improve being able to physically exert that kind of acceleration or high-speed running into a game.

"Then make a decision and to do it in a cool, calm manner and potentially have to make a VAR announcement and sound completely like they haven't been running around for 90 minutes."

The work pays off with Barrott recalling an incident in a match between Brighton and Fulham which underlined why it is worth it.

It came in March 2025 when he awarded a late penalty after Harrison Reed fouled Joao Pedro and the striker scored the injury-time penalty to earn the Seagulls a 2-1 win.

"I'm stood at the edge of the box, everyone turns and you're pointing at the penalty spot. There wasn't anything in me that thought 'you've got that wrong'," says Barrott.

"It was complete confidence, all because I'm stood in the right spot and to do that. It involves a little bit of football knowledge, anticipating what could happen and what we would call a danger area.

"But then also knowing what you've done for weeks and weeks - and potentially years and years - has allowed you to move into that position without having to think.

"It's just subconscious, it just happens and you're not stood there thinking: 'I'm tired, do I need to make that run?'

"That never comes into the thought process anymore, and the fatigue aspect of it never crosses your mind because we are where we need to be."

title: Why Spurs' under-the-radar buy might be summer's smartest deal
description: Why Kirsty Hanson's move from Aston Villa to Tottenham could be the key transfer of the Women's Super League summer.
fullText:
A number of stars from overseas have joined the Women's Super League this summer - but a move that has gone slightly under the radar could turn out to be more astute than them all.

Kirsty Hanson has swapped Aston Villa for Tottenham and there is reason to believe Spurs have quietly pulled off a recruitment masterstroke.

The 28-year-old was the third-highest goalscorer in the WSL last season despite the Scotland forward's side labouring in ninth place in the table.

With 12 goals in 22 matches, only PFA player of the year Khadija Shaw and England striker Alessia Russo scored more than her.

So why did Hanson make the move and how does she intend to take ambitious Tottenham - who start their WSL season on 6 September at home to West Ham - to another level this season?

How Tottenham's transfer window shows big WSL ambitions

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Fernandes and Shaw win PFA player of the year awards

It's true to say that Hanson's career really burst into life last season, but she had been steadily progressing throughout her successful four-year spell at Aston Villa.

Prior to that, she played a key role in Manchester United's development as a professional women's team before then struggling for regular game time.

When Villa brought her in initially on loan in 2022, Hanson was low on confidence and needed a boost.

With 26 goals in 100 appearances for Villa and two player-of-the-season awards, it's fair to say that happened.

"I've got to thank Villa so much. They know that I left on good terms. I really enjoyed my time," Hanson told BBC Sport.

"Everyone there helped me boost my confidence again. Hopefully, I can just build on that now, but I'm not putting pressure on myself.

"It was obviously a very tough decision to leave Villa but just looking at Spurs, you could see their ambition and each season they have been improving.

"When they appointed Martin [Ho] as manager, I think that was a big statement because he is one of the best coaches I've worked with."

Hanson worked with Ho during his time as assistant coach at United between 2020 and 2023.

He made Hanson a key target in this transfer window, and the club backed him by buying the striker for an undisclosed fee.

"I know he gets the best out of me with the detail he puts in. I really think that will push me further on in my career," added Hanson.

"The signings Tottenham have made shows they really want to push on and win things. I want to achieve that while I'm here.

"Training's been really tough. It was probably one of the toughest pre-seasons I've done so far. Martin is challenging us, trying to push us to our limits.

"That's what I really wanted, because I needed a challenge. I don't just want to be signed because they think I'm good, I want them to improve me."

New-look Villa turn to Scandinavia as they rebuild squad

FA approves WSL academy sides in National League

Having finished fifth last season, Tottenham are hoping to break into the WSL's top three and qualify for the Women's Champions League.

As well as Hanson, they have signed West Ham's top-scorer Shekiera Martinez, talented France defender Alice Sombath from Lyon and creative midfielder Victoria Pelova from rivals Arsenal this summer.

It means there will be fierce competition for a place in the starting XI - something Hanson is relishing.

"I'm definitely comfortable [in the WSL] now but I still don't see myself as one of the best. I'm very critical of myself," she said.

"It's going to be tough. I'm not expecting anything. My main aim is just to be better because I've got so many levels to go to. Martin knows that as well.

"I knew the level of players that were here. I'm just so excited to learn from them. I'm also here to help others, because that's what I've done at every club.

"I might not be the most talented but I've got a lot of fight and hunger in me. I literally run through a brick wall for my team. Hopefully I've showed them that."

Hanson's quality is unquestionable. Last season, she netted 43% of Villa's total goals and had the best shots on target ratio (50%) of the top-five goalscorers in the league.

She not only scored the bulk of Villa's goals, but only two team-mates created more chances than Hanson's 16 - and she had the most touches in the opposition box.

Her work-rate was evident too, as Hanson ranked among the top performers in her position in most defensive actions including tackling and interceptions.

The Scotland forward says she has also matured off the pitch and has a degree in sports coaching she hopes to put to good use.

Asked about where specifically she has developed, Hanson said: "I know what to do at different points in the game. I know how to calm players down.

"Previously when I worked with Martin, I was younger and I wouldn't have been able to cope with that as much. But now I've definitely matured a lot."

title: EFL weekend preview: Managers under pressure already
description: BBC Sport picks out five highlights to keep an eye on in Saturday's busy EFL programme.
fullText:
We may only be three weeks into the new EFL season but you can sense there is already a little twitchiness among some fanbases.

Not winning either of your first couple of league games brings unwanted attention - just ask West Ham, Stoke, Norwich and Burnley.

In League One, Plymouth Argyle's slow start last season ultimately cost them at least a play-off spot and it has been another sluggish opening as they prepare to host a buoyant Bradford City.

Salford City and Gillingham have been big spenders in recent seasons in League Two and yet remain mired in the fourth tier with their respective starts hardly giving cause for optimism - here are five things we have picked out to keep an eye on in the EFL this Saturday.

Relegation from the Premier League is only temporary, right? I mean, teams who come down go straight back up don't they?

Try telling that to Stoke City fans who are watching their team play Championship football for the ninth successive season, with a highest finish of 14th since dropping out of the top flight.

That did seem to be changing last season when, just over a third of the way through the campaign, they were second with a play-off place at the very least seeming inevitable.

But three wins from their final 20 games put those hopes to bed and this season has started with defeats by Swansea and Southampton.

But it is not for the want of trying by the Potters' owners, who continue to stump up the cash for signings to try to get them out of the Championship, with Ipswich's George Hirst arriving on a permanent deal and team-mate Ben Johnson coming in on a season-loan within the past fortnight.

Mark Robins is the seventh manager to attempt to get Stoke motoring again but that finish to last season and the start to this one has left some restless in their seats - a visit to Wolves on Saturday (12:30 BST) may not help things either.

If you were searching for optimism at the start of the season then you could have looked no further than Norwich City.

Relegation fodder when Philippe Clement took over in November, they eventually finished ninth, winning 17 of 31 league games that the Belgian took charge of.

A summer of careful transfer business including the likes of winger Andre Brooks from Sheffield United after already adding the impressive Ali Ahmed and Mohamed Toure in the new year window pointed towards a promotion challenge.

We may only be two games in but a home defeat by West Brom and a horror display at Millwall leaves them with no points and some head scratching to do.

Relegated Burnley head to Norfolk on Saturday (15:00 BST) and the Clarets are hardly enjoying their return to the Championship under new boss Nicky Hayen, with last weekend's loss at West Brom followed by a midweek EFL Cup exit at Bradford City.

There is still plenty of time for these two to get it right but time is a commodity not often afforded Championship managers.

Yes, we are talking about West Ham United again - they are difficult not to talk about at the moment.

Ownership wrangles and on-field failures make the perfect cocktail for endless headlines and stories.

Breaking the Championship transfer record to sign forward Arne Engels, and then for boss Nuno Espirito Santo to say it is with a view to him playing in the Premier League only draws more attention and pressure.

Losing at home to Charlton last weekend increased that pressure to a level that an EFL Cup win at Southampton on Tuesday will have done little to dampen.

Suddenly a short trip to Watford on Saturday (15:00 BST) looks to be littered with potential pitfalls, more so given the Hornets were themselves impressive winners over Southampton on the opening weekend before earning a notable draw at Wrexham.

Alessio Dionisi's much-changed side may have been thrashed at home by Peterborough in the EFL Cup in midweek but they seem to already have the taste for ruffling the feathers of those more fancied sides. West Ham beware.

Less patient owners may already have Tom Cleverley in the 'former Plymouth manager' bracket but those in south Devon are willing to take a longer-term view it would seem and that stance almost paid off last season.

Fourth from bottom in League One at the turn of the year, Argyle went into the final day of last season still in with a shot at the play-offs before having to settle for eighth place.

So, much like Norwich in the Championship, the start of this season was filled with optimism - but an opening day home defeat by Stockport and a point at Wycombe has reminded fans League One is a tough nut to crack.

It will not get any easier on Saturday (15:00 BST) when Bradford City come calling.

Fresh from reaching the play-offs last season after promotion from League Two, the Bantams have opened their campaign with wins over Peterborough and Sheffield Wednesday plus an EFL Cup upset victory against Burnley - all without conceding a goal.

The bigger they are, the harder they fall - a saying Salford City and Gillingham fans would do well to heed.

Two of League Two's bigger spenders in recent seasons, they are already finding the target on their backs a heavy one to carry.

The Ammies have paid undisclosed fees to tempt both Luke Molyneux (Doncaster) and Brendan Wiredu (Plymouth) to drop down from League One and try to finally help get them out of the fourth tier where they have been since promotion in 2019.

New boss Peter Cklamovski left his role as Malaysia's head coach to join Salford in June and defeats by Barnet and Chesterfield mean a win against pointless Shrewsbury on Saturday (15:00 BST) would steady the nerves a little.

A dozen new summer signings to go with splashing the cash on striker Ronan Hale in January has given Gillingham boss Gareth Ainsworth what he is calling 'his team' and 'his era.' Now they just need to start winning.

The past two seasons have seen the Gills start strongly but subside to successive 17th-place finishes.

Maybe this year will be different given they have taken only one point from two games and were trounced 3-0 at home by Walsall on a sobering first day.

Relegated Northampton head to Priestfield on Saturday (15:00 BST) in a similar situation under new head coach Chris Hogg.

BBC Sport will have live text coverage of all the weekend's EFL action starting with Wrexham v Birmingham City on Friday (20:00 BST).

title: Fery beats Kovacevic to reach Winston-Salem semi-final
description: Britain's Arthur Fery comes from a set down to beat Aleksandar Kovacevic and book his place in the semi-finals of the Winston-Salem Open.
fullText:
Britain's Arthur Fery came from a set down to beat Aleksandar Kovacevic and book his place in the semi-finals of the Winston-Salem Open.

Fourth seed Fery, who won five games in a row from 5-5 in the second set, claimed a 3-6 7-5 6-3 victory in Thursday's last-eight match in North Carolina.

After breaking Kovacevic to take the second set, Fery opened up a 3-0 lead in the third, serving out to clinch his first semi-final appearance since Wimbledon in July.

The 24-year-old will face James Duckworth, who he beat in Cincinnati earlier this month, in the last four, after the Australian defeated Hungarian 15th seed Fabian Marozsan 6-7 (4-7) 6-2 6-4.

Fery's surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals this summer lifted him into the top 40 in the world rankings - he is now 37th - and with it a place in the US Open for the first time.

He just missed out on being seeded for the final Grand Slam of the year at Flushing Meadows in New York so has been drawn against 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti in the opening round.

Alcaraz starts US Open comeback against Safiullin

'A generational icon' - why wildcards abound for Venus Williams

Also on Thursday, six British players were due to play their final US Open qualifying matches but heavy rain led to ties being suspended and postponed to Friday.

Jacob Fearnley is trailing Austria's Jurij Rodionov 3-2 in the deciding set after winning the first 6-4, but losing the second set by the same scoreline.

Harry Wendelken is up in the second set 5-4 after dropping the first 6-7 (3-7) to Lithuanian Vilius Gaubas, but Heather Watson, Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones did not get on court.

Toby Samuel, however, reached the main draw of the US Open for the first time after his opponent, Chile's Cristian Garin, retired during the break in play.

title: Southampton deny Spygate link to cuts to women's side
description: Southampton Women's head coach Simon Parker reveals that the summer has been "challenging" for the women's set-up at the club.
fullText:
Women's Super League 2 side Southampton have had their budget cut significantly after a "challenging" summer, according to head coach Simon Parker.

As part of the changes, the women's team will now play the majority of their matches at Eastleigh FC's Silverlake Stadium, instead of at St Mary's Stadium where they had spent the previous four seasons.

With the new campaign starting a week on Sunday, Parker told BBC Radio Solent they are now operating with the smallest budget in the WSL 2, and this has had a significant impact on their strategy for 2026-27.

"The summer has been a bit challenging with a few of the things that have happened," Parker said.

Sources at Southampton deny that these budget cuts are related to the spygate scandal.

Saints' men were removed from the Championship play-offs last season after the club admitted to spying on rival teams and started this season on minus four points.

In 2025-26, Southampton's women were in the mix for promotion to the WSL, ultimately finishing fifth, their highest position in the football pyramid since re-forming as a club nine years ago.

"It was a strong first year last season where the aim was always to try and finish in the top half and finishing fifth in a promotion push for a large part of the season was really promising," Parker added.

"Off the back of last season, the plan was to re-engage with a lot of our key players but we had to pivot and go into a different direction."

Earlier this summer, it was also revealed director of football Marieanne Spacey-Cale would step down, having been instrumental in the rise of the women's team at Southampton.

Spacey-Cale to step down at Southampton

Over the past few years, Saints have sold a number of their best players and that trend has continued.

Notable departures in recent years include Lucia Kendall who joined Aston Villa in 2025 and Kayla Rendell who signed for Manchester United in the same window.

Goalkeeper Fran Stanton left the club this summer alongside captain Atlanta Primus, Aimee Palmer and Tara Bourne.

Southampton have played all of their home matches at St Mary's Stadium since winning promotion to the second tier in 2022.

This change in ground will see them move from the 30,000-plus capacity arena to National League side Eastleigh's ground, which can hold just over five thousand fans.

Despite the downsize in grounds, Parker is looking at the positives and new opportunities that the move will bring.

"One of the ideas is they want to try and generate a tighter atmosphere," he added.

"When you play in a smaller stadium that can help with that, I do believe also that if you are playing in the main stadium truthfully, it does cost a lot of money.

"I would love for us to be playing at St Mary's every single week and I love it when we're there, we still have at least three games there this season.

"The definitive reasons (for the move) are not conversations that I'm part of."

Southampton begin their WSL 2 season at Durham on Sunday, 6 September (12:00 BST).

title: Why wildcards abound for Venus Williams
description: Venus Williams has not won a singles match in over a year but has received numerous wildcards to compete. The reasons why go beyond just tennis.
fullText:
Venus Williams has broken many acres of new ground as a tennis player, with five Wimbledon singles titles among her multiple achievements.

The 46-year-old has been playing professionally for nearly 30 years, but her last 14 singles matches have all ended in defeat.

With a world ranking of 611, Williams is reliant on wildcards to compete.

She has had 11 already this season - and the United States Tennis Association (USTA) has offered her a 12th so she can play at the US Open, where she will face fellow Grand Slam champion Sofia Kenin in the first round.

There is a school of thought that argues that, without any wins, it is simply too many, irrespective of her previous achievements.

But there is no limit to the number of wildcards a Grand Slam champion can receive and, for many tournaments, having a Williams sister on site still makes commercial sense.

"I think it's good for tennis to have these generational icons," said Karl Hale, the tournament director who offered Williams a wildcard for this month's WTA 1000 event in Toronto.

"That they are still allocating wildcards for them says something to their intrinsic value to the tournaments."

How to follow US Open on the BBC

Two-time US Open singles champion Williams has not qualified for a Grand Slam by ranking since Wimbledon 2021, which is also where she recorded her most recent singles win at a major.

She has been competitive in her past two Slam singles matches, pushing 11th seed Karolina Muchova to three sets in New York last year, and narrowly losing in three sets to Olga Danilovic at January's Australian Open.

Williams was also a doubles quarter-finalist at last year's US Open, but the defeat by qualifier Emiliana Arango in Cincinnati this month was her 18th loss in 19 singles matches. The only bright spot has been a win over Peyton Stearns in Washington last July.

And yet this year alone tournament directors in New Zealand, Australia, Spain, Germany and Canada - as well as the United States - have wanted Williams at their events.

Eight of the 128 spots in a Grand Slam singles draw are assigned to wildcards, and usually between four and eight at WTA and ATP events depending on the size of the field.

"The way we looked at Venus is that her legacy is phenomenal," Hale told BBC Sport.

"She's done so much for the sport and is really popular here in Toronto and our markets specifically - so we thought it was really good to announce it early that we have a Williams sister coming."

Hale says the media interest was significant, which he believes in turn drives ticket sales.

"The wildcards always play first-round matches, and with the bigger draw [size] now, it adds more notable names and stars for the beginning of the tournament," he said.

"Venus played opening day. She kicked off our tournament, so it added a lot of value."

Most tournaments will prioritise their own national players for wildcards, but they are also given to names who are likely to add commercial value to the event.

There are also what Hale calls 'trades' with other national federations or agencies like IMG, which manages players and until recently also owned the Miami and Madrid Opens.

The most obvious example of a 'trade' is the reciprocal wildcard agreement between the USTA, Tennis Australia and the French Tennis Federation. Each of these Grand Slam nations offers a men's and a women's wildcard to the others, knowing two of their players will benefit when it is their counterparts' turn to host.

One sporting event which has reduced the opportunity for past champions to return is the Open Golf Championship.

Twenty years ago, any champions under 65 could play whenever they wished. Now, winners only get the chance to return until they are 55, which could open up the odd place in the field to younger, more highly ranked professionals.

Golfers can be competitive for much longer, but there are no limits in tennis. Martina Navratilova was given a wildcard for both the 2004 French Open and Wimbledon - and won a round on the grass - when she made a comeback aged 47.

"You never want to put a player out there that you are unsure about," said Hale, who believes Williams is still capable of winning matches.

"Venus lost 6-4 6-1 to Kamilla Rakhimova, and the first set was really competitive. She's still competitive, but just not winning these matches."

So should there be a limit; a moment when a tournament director offers the spot to a more highly ranked player trying to advance their career?

"When the time comes that Venus is not competitive in sets, then I think she will make that call," Hale responded.

"Venus and Serena have done so much for women's tennis and the sport that they should be able to play as long as they want.

"I'm very happy they are continuing and they make their decision when they are ready, or each tournament makes their decision when they are ready."

British number one Katie Boulter put it a similar way after she partnered the "absolute icon" in the Madrid doubles in April.

"Venus has given so much to our sport that she deserves to get what she needs back," she said then.

"We have to be grateful that she is still out there, doing the best she can."

title: Hundred schedule impact worth the price - ECB chair
description: Scheduling issues caused by The Hundred are a "price worth paying", says England and Wales Cricket Board chair Richard Thompson.
fullText:
Scheduling issues caused by The Hundred are a "price worth paying", says England and Wales Cricket Board chair Richard Thompson.

The introduction of The Hundred in 2021 squeezed the domestic and international calendar in England, with just two days between the Hundred final and the first Test against Pakistan this summer.

While the ECB has ceded some control to new owners and investors and the addition of future teams remains a possibility, Thompson reiterated the stance that the number of days The Hundred is played across will not grow and said the current positives outweigh the negatives.

"Sacrifices have got to be made," he told Sky Sports.

"If we can take all of the debt out of the game, which we have, make a generation [of counties] which can reinvent themselves, that is a price worth paying."

What has been the impact of new owners on The Hundred?

More than £500m was raised when stakes in the eight Hundred franchises were sold last year - money that has been spread across the professional and domestic game.

Some counties have used the funds to clear debts or invest in infrastructure.

But to maximise the tournament's appeal, a window in July and August has been cleared of international cricket so that England's players are available for their franchises.

England are no longer able to pull their players out of The Hundred to prepare for international matches and bowler Josh Tongue described the turnaround as "crazy scheduling".

"We were criticised that The Hundred finished and two days later we were playing a Test match at Headingley," Thompson said.

"Imagine if that becomes one day - that can't happen."

The Hundred has also added to the congested domestic calendar which includes the County Championship, the T20 Blast and the One-Day Cup, which is now played beneath the Hundred, often as a second-team competition.

"We are having to crowbar so much cricket in," Thompson said.

"There are only four countries in the world that have managed to create a window that can pretty much guarantee the financial success of their game - us, South Africa, India, Australia."

Thompson also described the continued questions around the professionalism of England's men's team as "enormously" disappointing.

Bowler Brydon Carse was left out England's for the second Test against Pakistan after being briefly arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly while on duty with Durham.

He was de-arrested but investigations by the police and Cricket Regulator remain ongoing. Images on social media showed Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers.

"When you play for your country you are judged by far higher standards," Thompson said.

"What comes with wearing those three lions comes with respect, responsibility and pride.

"Unless you live and breathe those qualities there is a problem.

"Every player has to understand the responsibility that comes with playing for England."

title: Will fast-tracked Itauma become world champion at 21?
description: Can heavyweight Moses Itauma become world champion at 21 by beating Filip Hrgovic on Saturday or has the fast-tracked Briton arrived too soon?
fullText:
British heavyweight Moses Itauma pulls out his phone and scrolls through his pictures.

He shows a meme featuring former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo in traditional attire, standing with his hands on his hips and staring deadpan into the camera.

"This is how an African dad looks at you when you pursue a career that goes against his wishes and you turn out to be successful," a chuckling Itauma reads aloud to BBC Sport. "That is pretty much my dad."

Itauma was born in Slovakia to a Nigerian father and a Slovak mother before moving to Kent as a young child.

His parents originally wanted him to become a doctor or a lawyer. But once his older brother turned professional and the family recognised Itauma's exceptional natural talent, their stance softened.

"Don't worry about school. Just focus on your boxing," his mother eventually said.

That decision has paid off spectacularly.

At 21, Itauma steps into the ring against Filip Hrgovic on Saturday for the vacant IBF title with the chance to become the second-youngest world heavyweight champion in history.

"There's a lot of expectations on my shoulders to carry the flag of British boxing. I just have to live up to it," Itauma says.

Victory against Croatia's Hrgovic would put Itauma on the path to becoming the next big name in British heavyweight boxing, with Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua inching closer to the end of their storied careers.

Fury, with his Netflix documentaries and larger-than-life personality, has always made himself the attraction. Itauma is more like Joshua - guarded and keeping the media at arm's length.

"What irritates me most is when people think you're public property," he says.

"What people don't know about me is that I don't actually want to be in the limelight. The way my career is going, I just have no choice."

Like Joshua, Itauma often appears uninterested in the theatrics of fight week. When Hrgovic interrupted during Thursday's news conference, Itauma calmly asked host Adam Smith for the next question.

There are similarities in their careers, too.

Joshua fought Charles Martin for the IBF title in his 16th pro bout, having boxed 34 rounds. Itauma arrives at his first world-title opportunity a fight sooner and with 31 rounds logged.

While Joshua had an Olympic gold medal and a deeper amateur background, victory for Itauma would make comparisons unavoidable - eclipsing Joshua to become the fastest British heavyweight to win a world title.

Itauma's trainer Ben Davison, who also worked with Joshua and Fury, believes he has the temperament to handle what comes next.

"Pressure is a privilege," he says.

"Moses has already had that pressure for such a long time and I just think it's water off a duck's back."

Boxing's best young prospects tend to be handled carefully and are given time to learn before dangerous tests arrive.

Itauma, however, has been fast-tracked to his world-title shot.

Francis Warren - son of Queensberry chief Frank - first noticed him as a teenager, sparring established professionals. Former British heavyweight champion Jeamie 'TKV' Tshikeva was there even earlier.

"Moses was a big 11 or 12-year-old, around 75 to 80kg, (11st 11lb to 12st 8lb) and sparred an adult of the same weight," TKV says. "He really showed up, put hands on this grown man, and I was shocked.

"The guy he sparred was around 25. Imagine going home and telling your wife you got beat up by a kid."

Itauma's progress has been marked by destructive stoppages over Dillian Whyte and Jermaine Franklin. They may not be world-beaters, but the manner of those wins strengthened belief Itauma was destined for the top.

When Oleksandr Usyk vacated the IBF title and Frank Sanchez agreed to step aside, Itauma's fight with Hrgovic was elevated into a world-title contest.

Suddenly, the fast track looked, to some, like a shortcut.

Hrgovic - even before the IBF belt was on the line - claimed Itauma had been handed "everything on a plate". On social media, there was a similar feeling - perhaps a final eliminator would have been a more natural way to earn his shot.

Itauma, though, has little interest in proving himself to the doubters.

"It's a lose-lose situation for me because if I win, I've done what people expect, and if I lose, it's just like, I wasn't as good as what I thought," he says.

"I don't find happiness in trying to please other people's expectations."

Mike Tyson's mark as the youngest heavyweight champion in history - 20 years, four months and 22 days - remains boxing's ultimate holy grail.

While that record has passed, victory over Hrgovic would make Itauma the second-youngest heavyweight champion ever and boxing's youngest active world champion.

The Chatham heavyweight has never fought 12 rounds. He has never even sparred 12.

"Although I haven't gone 12 rounds and I haven't taken one on the chin, I don't think that's a characteristic you need to become a heavyweight champion," he says.

But what happens when his power does not end the fight? What happens when an opponent is still standing in round eight, still dangerous, still coming back?

TKV, who has sparred Joshua, Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley, has seen enough behind closed doors to believe Itauma can handle it.

"Moses works hard even though he hasn't had to face adversity in his fights or training," he says. "I've never seen him slack. He's fast, sharp, a good learner and I rarely see him get hit.

"I believe he can do the rounds, too. He has the potential to dominate the division for years."

There is no doubt within Itauma's camp that he belongs at this level. But all the outside questions over timing, merit and readiness will fade when the first bell sounds.

On Saturday, the prodigy has 12 rounds - if he needs them - to write his own chapter in heavyweight history.

title: O'Neill hopeful on transfers despite Champions League play-off exit
description: Celtic manager Martin O'Neill hopes missing out on the Champions League will not mean missing out on prospective targets.
fullText:
Manager Martin O'Neill hopes missing out on the Champions League will not mean Celtic miss out on prospective signings.

O'Neill's side will feature in the Europa League after Tuesday's 5-1 defeat by LASK after extra time, with the Austrian side winning the Champions League play-off 5-4 on aggregate.

The Scottish Premiership holders have signed four players so far this window, which closes next week.

"I'm hoping that's not the case," O'Neill said, when asked about the possibility of missing out on players.

"We're still trying to get some players in, we would need a few in obviously to supplement the squad.

"I'm hoping that we can get some people in before the transfer deadline."

Celtic face Benfica & Hearts meet Trabzonspor

Visit our Celtic page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

Celtic have faced criticism from supporters since last summer for the business done - or lack of it - in advance of the Champions League play-offs, which they also lost last season against Kairat Almaty.

Kasper Hogh, Camilo Duran, Haissem Hassan and Mika Baur all arrived at Parkhead before the LASK tie, but influential players Daizen Maeda and Arne Engels left for Ipswich Town and West Ham United, respectively.

"The Champions League is a big carrot for, particularly a lot of younger players," O'Neill said.

"The prestige is not there the same [in the Europa League], it's still a great competition. Obviously, the finance is still the big thing."

Reflecting on "the major disappointment" of Tuesday's loss, O'Neill admitted Celtic "should've been out of sight by half-time", at which stage they led 4-1 on aggregate.

"We did not do well in the second half," O'Neill explained

"The result's the most important thing and we got beaten. I'm obviously disappointed with myself. I have to really analyse it again.

"We could've maybe defended our box a wee bit better. I have to look at my own part before I look at anybody else's.

"You have to recover pretty quickly. You really have to. We have to show real character."

title: Netherlands beat Scotland by 58 runs in first ODI
description: The Netherlands comfortably beat a youthful Scotland side to take the lead in a three-match ODI series.
fullText:
First one-day international, Titwood

Netherlands 270-4 (50 overs): Molkenboer 106, De Leede 69; Maqsood 1-35

Scotland 212-10 (48.5 overs): Sproul 79, McColl 33; Siegers 3-42

The Netherlands comfortably beat a youthful Scotland side to take the lead in a three-match ODI series.

Having won the toss, stand-in Scotland captain Abtaha Maqsood opted to bowl at Clydesdale Cricket Club but the hosts struggled to make inroads on a good pitch.

Maqsood dismissed Sanya Khurana for 46 to get Scotland on the board. However, fellow opener Phebe Molkenboer amassed a superb 106 - her first ODI hundred - as the Dutch set 270-4 in their 50 overs.

Babette de Leede made 69 and Robine Rijke 18 in an impressive batting effort.

Without the likes of key players Kathryn and Sarah Bryce, Kirstie Gordon and Katherine Fraser, Scotland handed debuts to Charlotte Nevard and Rebecca McCrossan.

However, both failed with the bat in their first international outings as Nevard was trapped lbw first ball by Caroline de Lange and McCrossan was bowled by Khurana for five.

Hampshire wicketkeeper Pippa Sproul made 79 but Scotland fell 58 short of their target.

The next two fixtures are on Sunday and Tuesday, both at Stirling County Cricket Club.

The series was arranged at short notice as the Netherlands seek to regain their ODI ranking and avoid a substantial funding cut next year.

title: Man Utd sign Swedish winger Jusu Bah for £400k
description: Manchester United have confirmed the signing of Sweden winger Monica Jusu Bah from BK Hacken for just under £400,000.
fullText:
Manchester United have signed Sweden winger Monica Jusu Bah from BK Hacken for just under £400,000.

The 23-year-old joins on a four-year deal and becomes United's third signing before Thursday's Women's Super League transfer window deadline.

Jusu Bah was under contract until 2028 at Swedish club BK Hacken and United sources say they faced competition for her signature.

"It's an unbelievable feeling to join Manchester United," she said.

"There is a real togetherness in the group and you can feel the excitement from everyone for a big season ahead.

"The opportunity to work with Eva Olid is perfect. Everybody knows the quality of her coaching and her ability to support players to reach their highest level.

"I'm ready to keep pushing myself, help the team achieve our ambitions together and create special memories at this incredible club."

She has played in Sweden for her entire career, breaking through at Umea before moving to BK Hacken in 2023.

In May, Jusu Bah helped BK Hacken win the inaugural Women's Europa Cup.

She has made 11 appearances for Sweden and played in all six of their Women's World Cup qualifying matches this year.

It is understood United hope to add at least one more player before next week's deadline.

United have signed defender Andrea Medina from Atletico Madrid and goalkeeper Janina Leitzig from Leicester City.

title: Trabzonspor reject manager's 'emotional' resignation
description: Trabzonspor say Fatih Tekke's decision stems from the "intense emotional impact" of the Europa League exit.
fullText:
Trabzonspor have rejected the "emotional" resignation of head coach Fatih Tekke after the Turkish side, who signed Mohamed Salah in the summer, were knocked out of the Europa League on Thursday.

The Super Lig team suffered a 4-0 defeat by Ferencvaros in Hungary to lose the play-off tie 5-0 on aggregate.

In the aftermath, Tekke, who led Trabzonspor to a third-place finish in the league last season, tendered his resignation.

But that was rejected by the club on Friday, with the club saying the 48-year-old's decision stemmed from the "intense emotional impact" of the Europa League exit.

Salah said despite the "disappointment" of the defeat by Ferencvaros, he believed Trabzonspor "will deliver".

"Nothing in my career ever came easy. Bad nights and disappointments are part of football, and I have learned to turn them into motivation and into trophies," he wrote on X.

Sunderland and Bournemouth draw AC Milan in Europa League

"Trabzonspor is my club, and I am part of this project, body and soul. Last night will not change that.

"I know expectations are high, and I truly believe we can and will deliver. 'I came here to win' is not just a slogan to me."

Trabzonspor will instead compete in the Europa Conference League this season, with Scottish side Hearts among their six opponents.

The seven-time Turkish champions have been busy in the transfer market this summer, signing Premier League winners Salah and Fabinho. Andre Onana has also rejoined the club on loan from Manchester United.

Salah, 34, made the shock decision to sign for Trabzonspor last month after mutually agreeing to end his contract at Liverpool last season.

The Egypt international is the third-highest scorer in the Reds' history, behind only Ian Rush and Roger Hunt, after scoring 257 goals in 442 appearances following his move from Roma in 2017.

Salah scored his first two goals for his new club in Saturday's 2-1 win against Istanbul Basaksehir.

title: Asian Games hosts say all athletes will have rooms
description: The hosts of the Asian Games in Japan say all athletes will be provided with accommodation for next month's event, after fears there would be a shortage of rooms.
fullText:
The hosts of next month's Asian Games in Japan say all athletes will have accommodation for the event, after fears there would be a shortage of rooms.

Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials were expected to attend the Games, which will be held in the Nagoya and Aichi region between 19 September and 4 October.

However, last week the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included earlier this year.

In a joint statement, Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games Organising Committee (AINAGOC) and the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) said they wanted to clear up "incorrect media reports" regarding accommodation issues.

"All the 17,000-plus athletes and officials that are registered for the Asian Games before the closing of Entry by Name in July have been provided with Games-appropriate accommodation," it read.

"Unless there are exceptional circumstances, no further registrations have been or will be permitted."

The mayor of Nagoya and acting chairman of the local organising committee, Ichiro Hirosawa, had earlier said it was "difficult to accommodate this number" because the Games is "operating on a tight budget".

And Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, had said the hosts had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the late influx of athletes.

"The host city agreement specifies a delegation of 15,000 people," explained Omura. "We have not set aside a budget for any more than that.

"There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements."

However, in Friday's statement the organisers said: "The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations."

Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors.

Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes will stay on board the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena that will be docked in the area, while a further 2,000 will use shipping container-style huts.

The remaining athletes and officials will be accommodated in hotels in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events are scheduled to take place.

title: Simeone would welcome Alvarez back to training amid Barca row
description: Diego Simeone says he will do everything he can to make Julian Alvarez feel important at Atletico Madrid, after confirming the Argentina international will miss Saturday’s match against Sevilla.
fullText:
Diego Simeone says he will "do everything" he can to make Julian Alvarez "feel important" at Atletico Madrid when the forward returns to training, as uncertainty continues over his situation at the Spanish club.

It comes as Atletico Madrid made it clear that they would not sell him to Barcelona, with a move to Arsenal looking like the striker's only way out.

Simeone confirmed Alvarez will not travel with Atletico for Saturday's La Liga game at Sevilla saying he is not currently in good health, having missed his third consecutive training session on Friday.

"From the moment he returns to training, I will do everything I can to make him feel important," said Atletico manager Simeone.

Asked whether Alvarez's situation could still be reversed, Simeone added: "As long as you have your health, everything in life can be turned around."

This week the La Liga club released two public statements in the space of 24 hours reiterating their stance that Alvarez will not be granted his wish to join Barca in the coming days.

Simeone said he understood why questions about Alvarez would dominate his news conference but insisted the club had already been "forceful and clear" in explaining the situation.

"I'm still in the same position, hoping, from a sporting point of view, to be able to help him in the best way so that he continues to be the very important player he is for us," he said.

"Julian will not be there [on Saturday] against Sevilla, who have just won two games and will be high with confidence."

Injured Norwegian striker Alexander Sorloth is also unavailable, leaving Atletico without two attacking options.

"Sorloth's absence hurts us. He's very important for us," Simeone said.

"In this situation with Julian, it has much more impact. The team will try collectively to find solutions to score goals and win. We are working with them on that awareness. We are going to try to improve it collectively."

Simeone also rejected concerns that the uncertainty surrounding Alvarez could affect his squad.

"Honestly, no," he said. "The boys are working very well, especially the World Cup players. The team played good matches against Malaga and Villarreal and we are focused on playing a good match [against Sevilla]."

New defender Cristian Romero, who joined Atelti from Tottenham for 40m euros (£34.2m) this summer, will travel with the squad to Sevilla, although Simeone said: "He needs time to find his best form and we will not speed up the time to rush him, so that he feels that he is in a position to perform as well as he should."
